question: m09
q: Have building approvals picked up since the RBA started cutting?

transcript.answer:
Yes. Approvals have risen clearly since the RBA's first cut in February 2025, and they've stayed high even though the RBA has since raised rates again.

**The rates background:** The cash rate fell from 4.35% to 3.60% between February and August 2025. It stayed there until January 2026, then went back up from February 2026. It has been about 4.35% since June 2026, which means the cuts have been fully reversed.

**Dwelling approvals, Australia (ABS, number of dwellings).** The ABS figures I could get here aren't seasonally adjusted, so I've compared full 12-month totals rather than single months:

| 12 months to | Total dwellings | Houses | Apartments, townhouses etc. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2025 (before the cuts) | 176,596 | 111,788 | 64,808 |
| Aug 2025 | 190,089 | – | – |
| Aug 2026 (latest) | 208,145 | 124,307 | 83,838 |
| **Change since the cuts began** | **+17.9%** | **+11.2%** | **+29.4%** |

**Key points:**
- **Total approvals are up about 18%** on the year before the cuts. That's roughly 2,600 more dwellings a month (about 17,300 a month now versus 14,700).
- **Apartments and townhouses drove most of the rise (+29%)**. These figures jump around from month to month because a few large projects can swing them.
- **Houses rose more steadily (+11%)**. Every month from March to August 2026 had more than 10,400 house approvals, a level only reached twice in the year before the cuts.
- **The rise continued after rates started going up again.** February–August 2026 approvals totalled 127,530, which is 12.2% more than the same months of 2025 (113,662).
- **August 2026 was weaker than July** (16,967, down from 19,273), mostly because apartment and townhouse approvals fell. It was still 10.3% higher than August 2025, and house approvals were up 14.4% on a year earlier. One month doesn't make a trend, but it's worth watching now that rates are back at 4.35%.

**Caveats:** Approvals usually respond to rate changes with a lag of several months to a year, so the recent hikes may not show up yet. These figures also don't show how much of the rise came from cheaper borrowing rather than other factors, such as government housing targets and help for first-home buyers.
